summary: Describes what robust header compression expects from the link layers beneath it, and what those layers should do to support it. It is aimed at people incorporating ROHC into systems such as those defined by 3GPP, 3GPP2 and ETSI, so that compressed headers work well over cellular and similar links.

eli5.summary: Squeezing the address labels on messages only works if the road underneath cooperates. This note tells the people building those roads what the label-squeezing system needs from them.

subtitle: What link layers need to do to support robust header compression

tldr.problem: Robust header compression (ROHC) algorithms reduce bandwidth by compressing RTP/UDP/IP headers, but they depend on the underlying link layer to provide certain capabilities that are not always present in cellular systems.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies what lower layer functionality ROHC requires: error detection, packet ordering, feedback channels, and strategies for handling variable header sizes and handovers in cellular networks.
tldr.outcome: Cellular system designers know what to implement to support ROHC efficiently, allowing voice, video, and real-time traffic to consume less bandwidth.

today: RFC 3409 remains relevant for any cellular or mobile system implementing header compression. 3GPP and 3GPP2 systems have incorporated ROHC and follow these guidelines. The document serves as a design checklist for link layer implementations and helps ensure that ROHC deployments achieve their bandwidth-saving goals. As cellular networks continue to evolve, these principles remain applicable for incorporating efficient header compression.

sections.title: Header Compression and Link Layer Requirements
sections.content:
Header compression is a technique to reduce bandwidth by replacing redundant fields in packet headers with shorter markers. The Robust Header Compression (ROHC) algorithm, defined in RFC 3095, is designed to work reliably even on cellular links with high error rates.

Like all header compression schemes, ROHC assumes certain capabilities from the lower layers beneath it. If those capabilities are missing or inadequate, ROHC cannot work correctly. This RFC documents what ROHC requires, helping designers of cellular systems (such as those standardized by 3GPP and 3GPP2) and other link layers incorporate ROHC support.

The key insight is that ROHC was designed not to increase the bit error rate in headers compared to uncompressed transmission. However, this design assumption depends on the link layer doing its part.
sections.eli5: Compressing headers saves bandwidth, but it only works if the network underneath provides certain things. This document lists what it needs.

sections.title: Core Requirements for All Link Layers
sections.content:
Several requirements apply to any link layer using ROHC:

Error Detection: All previous header compression schemes assumed the link layer would detect errors in headers using checksums or similar mechanisms. ROHC has the same assumption. The link layer must detect errors in (compressed) headers so they can be discarded or passed up with an error indication. Because no error detection is perfect, residual bit errors (errors that slip through) may occur, but they must be kept to near zero for headers.

Inferring Header Fields: Some fields in the IP/UDP/RTP headers are redundant and can be inferred from other information. For example, the IP Payload Length field in the compressed packet can be inferred from the link layer's total packet length signal. By providing packet length information on a per-packet basis, the link layer eliminates the need for ROHC to transmit these fields.

Header Size Variation: Compressed headers vary in size, from as little as 1 byte (in steady state) up to 40 or 60 bytes (for full RTP/UDP/IPv4 or IPv6 uncompressed headers sent during initialization). Link layers must support this variation. Many cellular systems prefer fixed-size packets, so ROHC provides options to pad headers and limit the number of different sizes used.

Parameter Negotiation: ROHC has configurable parameters, such as which compression profiles (algorithms for different header types) are allowed and what context identification (CID) mechanism to use. The link layer must provide mechanisms to negotiate these during setup, ensuring that compressor and decompressor use the same settings.

Feedback Channels: ROHC can operate in three modes. Unidirectional mode (U-mode) requires no feedback. Bidirectional optimistic (O-mode) and bidirectional reliable (R-mode) require feedback messages from decompressor to compressor. The link layer must support carrying these small feedback packets, either as standalone messages or piggy-backed onto data packets.

Packet Ordering: ROHC assumes packets between compressor and decompressor are not reordered. However, ROHC handles reordering before the compressor (i.e., at the source), so the compressor does not assume its input is ordered.

No Duplication: The link layer must not duplicate packets on the compression path, as this wastes bandwidth and defeats compression.
sections.eli5: The link layer must check for errors, tell the compressor how long packets are, handle variable sizes, let compressor and decompressor agree on settings, carry feedback messages, and not reorder or duplicate packets.

sections.title: Requirements for Cellular Systems
sections.content:
Cellular systems have additional characteristics that affect ROHC:

Handover Procedures: In cellular networks, devices move between base stations. A soft handover keeps radio connections to multiple sites simultaneously; a hard handover switches to a new site abruptly, potentially dropping packets temporarily. Long gaps in packet delivery due to hard handovers can desynchronize the compressor and decompressor—they lose context about what packets have been delivered and what state they should be in.

The RFC recommends minimizing consecutive packet loss during handover. If long loss events are unavoidable, the network should notify the ROHC compressor when a handover has occurred so it can refresh its context by sending full (uncompressed) headers, resynchronizing with the decompressor. Cellular systems can also transfer the compression context from the old base station to the new one, avoiding re-initialization.

Unequal Error Detection (UED): Some cellular link layers can apply different error detection strengths to different parts of a packet. For example, headers can be protected more strongly than the payload. ROHC does not require UED, but it can improve performance: if only the header is protected and a bit error hits the payload, the packet can still be delivered (the application may tolerate payload errors). With uniform error detection over the entire packet, a payload error causes the whole packet to be discarded.

Unequal Error Protection (UEP): Similarly, some links can provide different error protection (through coding or retransmission) for different parts. Stronger protection for headers can reduce the header error rate when combined with unequal error detection. UEP is not required but can improve performance.
sections.eli5: Cellular phones move between towers (handover), which can disconnect packets for a moment. The compressor needs to know when this happens so it can re-sync. Some cellular systems can protect headers more strongly than data, which helps compression work even better.

sections.title: Implications for System Design
sections.content:
This RFC is primarily a checklist for standardization groups and system designers. When a cellular standard like 3GPP or ETSI incorporates ROHC, it should ensure the link layer supports all these requirements. Without them, ROHC cannot deliver the bandwidth savings it promises.

The document emphasizes that preparation can proceed without knowing the exact details of the final ROHC specification, provided that these general guidelines are followed. A well-designed link layer that provides error detection, feedback paths, parameter negotiation, and handling for variable packet sizes will support ROHC regardless of minor changes to the ROHC algorithm.

The RFC also notes that the same principles apply to other link layers, such as PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol), though the specific mechanisms differ. For example, PPP already has mechanisms for parameter negotiation, so a PPP implementation of ROHC focus on error detection and feedback support.
sections.eli5: When engineers design a cellular system, they can use this list to make sure everything ROHC needs is built in. And the same ideas work for other types of networks too.
